details:
What it does
Going Beyond the Lens is a web app that shows what NISAR, the new NASA and ISRO L-band radar satellite, saw during Indonesia's 2026 peat fires. In September and October, VIIRS logged 160,910 fire detections around Pulang Pisau, Central Kalimantan, and the smoke blinded the camera satellites. Over our Pulang Pisau window, Landsat and Sentinel-2 got one usable look in 11 passes at the peak of the fires (15 September to 1 November). NISAR got an image on all 8 of its passes, because L-band radar passes through cloud and smoke.

How it works
A Python pipeline streams only the 22 km windows it needs from each NISAR GCOV scene over HTTPS, without downloading the full files. It covers eight windows in Kalimantan, Sumatra and Papua, each seen from two orbits. It averages the radar into 200 m cells and compares them with an optical burn map (dNBR from HLS Landsat and Sentinel-2) and with VIIRS hotspots. The app lets you drag a slider between any two radar dates and switch layers on and off: radar change, a fixed rule (the echo fell by 1 dB or more), hotspots and the burn map. It scores the change against the burn map live for whichever pair you pick. A filmstrip puts every radar pass next to the camera image from the same days.

What it found
In Pulang Pisau the HV channel separates burned from unburned ground with an AUC of 0.81 (95% interval 0.75 to 0.87). Pairs from before the fires score 0.45 to 0.51, which is no signal, as a control should show. When the 1 dB rule flags a cell, it is right 95% of the time, against 61% for a rule flagging cells at random. It raises 2.7% false alarms and catches 32% of burned cells, so it finds the core of the burn, not every edge. HH shows no burn signal in any window, which answers the challenge's polarization question. The method holds on Kalimantan peat, weakens in Sumatra and fails on Papua's savanna, and the app says so.

Benefits and intended impact
Indonesia's official burned-area map (SiPongi, Ministry of Forestry) is drawn on Landsat images, and at the peak of a fire season Landsat cannot see the ground. A radar layer gives mappers and fire responders a look at what burned during the weeks the camera is blind, not after the smoke clears.

What makes it different
Counted every optical pass instead of claiming the camera "saw only smoke": the camera did see the ground in August and early September. The app shows the placebo test beside the result, so a judge or user can check the claim instead of trusting it.

Tools

  • Pipeline: Python with asf_search, h5py, fsspec, rasterio, numpy, pandas, scipy and Pillow, managed with uv.
  • App and demo deck: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no libraries and no outside requests, hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Checks: Node.js tests that confirm the app's scores equal the pipeline's, GitHub Actions, and Playwright page checks.
  • AI: code were assisted with Claude (Anthropic), directed and checked by me. (no images were generated by AI)

Factors we considered
Since hotspots are not burned area I score against an optical map instead. The detection rule was fixed before scoring. Placebo pairs test whether the signal is real. The limits are stated on the page: eight windows, one fire season, mostly provisional radar data, and an optical truth map that was itself read through haze. It is a demonstration, not a burned-area product.
